newsitem.title: USA: Trial set Feb 1998 in L.A. Cty yield burning case.
newsitem.headline: Trial set Feb 1998 in L.A. Cty yield burning case.

text.p: A California Superior Court has set a Feb 27, 1998, trial date for Los Angeles County's "yield burning" legal challenge against Lazard Freres & Co, the county's outside lawyer John Phillips said.

The move comes after California's Supreme Court earlier this month rejected Lazard Freres' third and last possible motion to win dismissal of the case, Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority v Lazard Freres & Co.

The Supreme Court's decision opened the way for San Francisco County Superior Court to launch discovery proceedings in the case, which is the first challenge nationwide by a municipality involving yield burning.
Phillips, a partner with Phillips & Cohen in Washington, D.C., said attorneys in the case will meet shortly with whichever judge is appointed to the case to set a schedule for "discovery."
Discovery is the often contentious process by which each party in a case is compelled by the court to turn over documents and evidence to the other.

There will be "many battles along the way," said Phillips, noting that his firm has asked Lazard Freres to turn over pricing information for all Lazard Freres refinancings. It is unclear whether the request encompasses all of 1990 to 1995.
"They are saying this was consistent with our practice -- this is how we've been charging everybody," Phillips said. "Well okay," so turn over the data, he added.
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge states and localities for U.S. Treasury securities they bought to help them refinance outstanding bonds.
The county is charging that Lazard, which was financial adviser for authority refinancings from 1990 to 1995, illegally overprices Treasuries purchased by the authority.
The lawsuit was first filed by former municipal finance banker Michael Lissack under California's false claims statute.
The Los Angeles County authority joined the lawsuit eight months later. Phillips anticipated the trial will last two to three weeks.
